statement: Anas: he wrote to Chosroes, Caesar, the Negus and other rulers, calling them to Allah. The letter to Heraclius reached him during the truce of Hudaybiyyah.
notes: Sahih Muslim 1774a on Sunnah.com supports the recipients and invitation. Bukhari 7 places Heraclius's letter during the truce; extending that timing to every letter would be an inference. Human review remains required.

statement: Anas: told that the Romans do not read unsealed letters, he had a silver ring made, engraved 'Muhammad Rasul Allah'; Anas recalled its whiteness on his hand.
The text of the letter to Heraclius.
notes: Direct quotation. Machine-checked against the dataset text. 'The sin of your subjects' renders 'ithm al-arisiyyin', whose meaning the commentators discuss.

statement: Heraclius, in Jerusalem (Ilya), summoned Abu Sufyan's caravan and questioned him on lineage, kingship among his forefathers, lying, treachery, and his teaching; Abu Sufyan's answers; his remark that he would have lied but for shame before his companions.
notes: Direct speech, abridged. From Bukhari 7, used and partly machine-checked in chapters 2, 5 and 9.

statement: Heraclius said he would rule the ground under his feet, that he knew a prophet would appear but not from them, that he would strive to meet him and wash his feet; when his court was in uproar he did not follow through.
notes: Direct speech from memory of Bukhari 7; reviewer to check wording.

statement: Ibn Abbas: the letter to Chosroes was sent with Abdullah ibn Hudhafah via the governor of Bahrain; Chosroes tore it up; the Prophet prayed that they be torn apart completely.
notes: Machine-checked. The supplication is reported by the sub-narrator from Ibn al-Musayyab.

statement: Letters also went to al-Muqawqis of Egypt, who replied courteously with gifts, and to the Negus.
notes: The texts of these letters are transmitted by the historians; their chains are discussed by scholars. The gifts included Mariyah; not narrated here.

statement: The Sasanian empire fell within a generation.
notes: General history (the Muslim conquest of Persia was complete by about 651 CE).
